title_en: Cooking by Video: A Cautionary Tale
description_ru: Комичная история о том, как попытка приготовить «простое» блюдо по видеорецепту превращается в кухонную катастрофу.
text:
There is a particular sort of confidence that comes over a person at eleven o'clock on a Saturday night, in the glow of a laptop, after watching a stranger make a beautiful dish in nine minutes. It is the confidence of someone who has seen the finished article and assumed that the work in between would be pleasant. I know this confidence well, and I would like to warn you about it.

The video was called "Perfect Beef Wellington: Easy Enough for Beginners". The presenter, a man with strong forearms and a rustic apron, spoke in the gentle voice of someone who had never experienced a disappointment. "Honestly, it's just a few simple steps," he said, as he flicked a fillet of beef across a pan with one hand. I believed him. I had invited my in-laws for lunch on Sunday, my mother-in-law having once described my cooking as "brave", and I had decided that this was my moment to correct the record.

My first mistake was the shopping. The recipe called for "a good piece of centre-cut fillet", and in the shop I discovered that this phrase, which in the video cost nothing, translated in reality into a sum roughly equal to my monthly gas bill. The butcher, noticing my expression, asked kindly whether I was celebrating something. "A reputation," I said. He wrapped it very carefully, with the solemn manner of a man handing over a newborn.

By Sunday morning the kitchen was already in a condition that the presenter's kitchen never achieved at any stage. In the video, the work surfaces were bare, apart from a small bowl of salt and a single sprig of thyme arranged, I suspect, by a professional. In mine there were seven bowls, two chopping boards, a mound of mushrooms and a cat, who had arrived to supervise. The recipe instructed me to "finely chop the mushrooms until they resemble wet sand", which sounds quite easy, until you discover that mushrooms release a quantity of water that would embarrass a small river.

"Cook until all the moisture has evaporated," said the man in the video, with the serenity of one who had edited out forty minutes of waiting. I cooked for what felt like a geological era. The mushrooms stubbornly refused to dry, and I added a little more heat, which turned the mixture into something resembling a swamp, and then a little more, until it resembled a cremated swamp. At last I decided that this was what "wet sand" meant, and moved on.

The next step was the ham. The recipe suggested laying slices of Parma ham on cling film, spreading the mushroom paste over it, and then using the film to roll the beef into a tight, elegant cylinder. In the video, this took the presenter a moment and looked like wrapping a present. In my kitchen, the cling film adhered to everything except the beef. It clung to my fingers, my sleeves, the cat and, for a long and terrible interval, to my own face. I stood in the middle of the kitchen like a victim of a particularly adhesive crime, wondering whether it was legal to cry into a fillet worth forty pounds.

By the time I had constructed something that could generously be described as a log, my in-laws were due in an hour. The pastry was next. The recipe said, "Simply drape the puff pastry over the beef", with the casual air of someone describing the act of putting on a hat. The pastry, which I had taken out of the fridge too early, had developed the consistency of warm toffee. It tore. I patched it, using a second sheet, and then a third, until my Wellington resembled a quilt made by someone in great distress. I covered the worst of the damage with a pattern of leaves cut from the leftover scraps, which I felt gave the whole thing a certain rustic dignity.

The doorbell rang at precisely the moment when I discovered that I had forgotten to preheat the oven. I will not describe the next twenty minutes in detail, except to say that I greeted my in-laws with a smile I had borrowed from a hostage and offered them wine in large glasses. My father-in-law, a man of few words and fewer opinions, asked whether something was burning. "That," I said, "is the smell of ambition."

When the Wellington finally emerged, it was a striking object. The pastry on the top was a handsome golden brown. The sides, however, had split like a pair of tight trousers, and a slow tide of grey liquid was creeping across the dish towards the edge. I carried it to the table with the stately pace of a man bringing in a sacrificial offering, and everyone stared at it in silence.

It was, to my continuing astonishment, delicious. The beef was perfectly pink, and the mushrooms, which I had cooked for a geological era, had reached a depth of flavour that I would not have achieved on purpose. My mother-in-law took a second slice, chewed thoughtfully and looked at me with an expression I had not seen on her face before. "Well," she said at last, "I suppose that was brave."

I have thought about this many times since. The lesson, I believe, is not that video recipes lie, although they do, but that they omit the one ingredient on which all cooking depends, which is failure. Behind every nine-minute masterpiece there is a dustbin full of attempts and a producer who has gone to lunch. If I have learned anything, it is that the presenter's calm is a costume, and that the cat was right to supervise.
